512.prompt: I knelt beside the flowerbed and pressed the seed into the soil. Then I
512.completion:
dug a small hole and carefully covered my precious seed. It looked so insignificant. I couldn’t see what a magnificent flower it would become. Years of sunshine, rain showers, and tender loving care were necessary for it to grow into the beautiful bloom it would become.

When I looked at my fragile baby, I thought of all the seeds we have planted in our lives. Our children’s eyes are the size of their first peas in a pod. Then we love them, feed them, read to them, teach them, and—with God’s help—they grow up. I can picture my first child toddling down the hall with her little pink flowered pants and bare feet. My first thought was, “Oh, the trouble this one will cause!” I knew she wouldn’t be a flower to sit in the garden. She was a wild little weed. She should be trained early on.

How difficult it is for me to see the possibilities for each of my children. But because I believe in my heart that our children come from God, there is a divine seed planted in every one of us. If we nurture this seed, it must grow.

We cannot push it, bully it, scold it or prod it. However, with eternal parenting and loving parental guidance, our children will grow into the mighty oaks that God wants them to be. It is not our responsibility to create the fruit. Our responsibility as parents is to give our children the tools to develop the gifts God gave us.

The wise parent learns, teaches and waits. We give our children the tools of truth and the tools of hard times and experience. Then we patiently wait for the seeds to grow. It may take years, but as surely as sunflowers rise from the earth and fill the skies with sunshine, our children will become the flowers we planted them to be.<eos>

sanded down the rough edges of the wood, smoothed out the shelves, and then painted a new coat of primer. When the primer dried, he started to paint each coat of the final color. 

Sam was in the process of installing bookshelves across the country, so it was important to him to use the same primer and paint color at each site. He bought the materials at Home Depot to ensure the supplies were the most consistent from location to location.

However, as Sam began to pain the bookshelf, he noticed that the paint did not look right. It appeared patchy, lumpy, and discolored. He reexamined the instructions on the paint can, but it seemed like he had followed them correctly. 

It could have been that the paint itself had gone bad. However, when Sam checked the can, it read that it was good for 3 years, and it was just under a year old. 

What had gone wrong?

If you have ever painted a room, primed a wall to provide color uniformity, or replaced a broken piece of wood, then you have used paint that contains microemulsions. These oil and water solutions help to evenly spread and distribute the color on the substrate being painted. However, a study conducted by a group of researchers at NIST looked to uncover the exact cause (2). walked to the edge of the walkway.

“My name’s Rina and this is my garden,” she said to the woman with the sweeping brush. “I’m adding this, so you see, we can still keep the pavement.” She gestured at the sweepings in the small pile on the pavement.

The woman grunted. “You think you can claim the bit you’ve planted? It’s mine.” She gave Rina a hostile stare.

Rina was tempted to ignore her and put the next seed in the hole. But it wasn’t her right.

She shrugged. “You’re welcome to whatever you want. There’s just one thing.”

“What’s that?”

“Gardening is my therapy. I get up before the council sweepers get to me and I love to come out and garden.” She tapped the trowel.

“I work. You should be at work.”

“This is my work. If the council decides that my therapy is so valuable that I can’t do it any more, then I will have to look for a job. Until that time, I recommend you do the work you’re paid for.”

The woman snorted. Rina put the next seed in the hole and patted the soil in, then stood with her hands on her hips.

“It’s not your business whether I work or not,” she said. “Do you ever wonder why you’re bothered some days and other sweepers do the job, others of them completely normal and sensible?”

“What’s that got to do with it?”

“If the sweepers aren’t allowed to do their jobs, they’re off in a huff. They find you who don’t give a dam about anything.” She looked down at the woman’s uniform. The council logo had been crossed out in permanent marker.

The woman backed up slightly, hands on her hips, staring at Rina.

Rina stood with her hands on her hips. She looked into the woman’s face for a few moments. Then, she bowed slightly and swept an arm out in a slight gesture. This wasn’t a fight.

“Fine, if that’s the way you want it,” said the woman, and she moved on without sweeping.<eos>

The hardware store was too far away, too busy and too cold to drive to. “Well, we’ll see,” dad said. I didn’t like the sound of that. I threw the screws into the toolbox and carried it back to the garage. We set about cutting the final pieces for the bookshelf and proceeded to glue it together.
